name: Tewa
confidence_why: Speirs 1966, the only grammar of Tewa, reports decidedly heavier stress on the first syllable of level-toned CVCV nouns regardless of their position in the utterance and expressly rejects the equal-stress claim of Hoijer and Dozier 1949, a six-page preliminary sketch of the Santa Clara dialect based on a single bilingual speaker, while Sutton 2014 independently places Kiowa-Tanoan lexical stress on the first syllable of the stem.
catalog_quote: all two-syllable nouns of syllable pattern CVCV and tone pattern high-high or low-low show decidedly heavier stress on the first syllable than on the second--regardless of their position in the utterance, so that the weaker stress cannot be attributed to /#/.

new_statements.quote: 8. On the basis of stress and pitch accent it is possible to divide Santa Clara syllables into five types: high, middle, low, falling, and weak. Utterances which include syllables of the first four kinds alone are pronounced with about the same stress on each syllable; the only prosodic variation in such utterances is in respect to pitch accent. Weak syllables, on the other hand, have no discernible pitch accent but are markedly less stressed than pitch-accented syllables and, in rapid speech, may even be whispered. [...] Weak syllables never occur as free forms and usually are found at the ends of utterances.
new_statements.citation: Hoijer, Harry & Edward P. Dozier. 1949. The phonemes of Tewa, Santa Clara dialect. International Journal of American Linguistics 15(3): 139-144.
new_statements.locator: p. 143, section 8 'Stress and pitch' (PDF page 5 of the issue scan); the prosodic summary is on pp. 139-140, section 2
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (archive.org scan of IJAL 15(3), July 1949, 57 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'International Journal of American Linguistics 1949-07: Vol 15 Iss 3'); rendered PDF page 5 = printed p. 143 ('NO. 3 PHONEMES OF TEWA, SANTA CLARA DIALECT 143') and read it as an image, and checked the extracted text and layers ( lines 583-597). Section 8 'Stress and pitch' begins exactly: 'On the basis of stress and pitch accent it is possible to divide Santa Clara syllables into five types: high, middle, low, falling, and weak. Utterances which include syllables of the first four kinds alone are pronounced with about the same stress on each syllable; the only prosodic variation in such utterances…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records Tewa with the StressTyp2 initial stress (primary stress on the first syllable). Hoijer & Dozier report no such placement: all pitch-accented syllables of the Santa Clara dialect are pronounced with about the same stress and the only prosodic variation is tone (high/middle/low/falling); the one stress contrast is the weak, toneless, usually utterance-final syllable. That is a tone-plus-level-stress description, not initial word stress. Whether the StressTyp2 initial-stress entry rests on a later or different-dialect source could not be checked here (no other work was listed).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every syllable carries one of four tones (high, middle, low, falling) or is 'weak' (no tone, markedly less stress). Among toned syllables there is no stress difference: they are 'pronounced with about the same stress on each syllable', so there is no culminative word-stress position; the only prosodic variation is pitch. The one stress distinction is the weak syllable, which never stands alone, is usually utterance-final (e.g. the final syllable of pin-ge-he:-?i? 'halfwit', marked with a breve) and may be whispered in rapid speech. Section 2 (p. 139) states the same: 'stress accent (some rarely occurring syllables have a markedly weak stress), and pitch accent (except for weak-stressed syllables, each syllable has a low, high, middle, or falling tone)'; the authors add that they have no data on phrasal or sentence prosodics.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. The only gradation reported is toned (full-stress) versus weak syllables; no primary/secondary hierarchy.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak-stressed syllables (breve-marked; final syllables of certain polysyllabic forms such as the -?i?/-?ih nominal/verbal endings) are the only syllables with reduced stress; they never occur as free forms and are usually found at the ends of utterances. The falling tone occurs only on long-vowel or -n-closed syllables. The description rests on a single bilingual speaker (Dozier) and the authors call their conclusions preliminary (p. 139).
new_statements.identity_note: Hoijer & Dozier 1949 describe the Santa Clara Pueblo dialect only (Rio Grande Tewa, within tewa1260), from a single bilingual speaker (Edward P. Dozier); they note the San Juan, San Ildefonso, Tesuque, Nambe, Pojoaque and Hano (Arizona Tewa) varieties as mutually intelligible dialects but give no prosodic data for them. The listed open_url (WALS refdb record 360) is the wrong item: it is Holmer 1949, 'Goajiro (Arawak) I: Phonology' (IJAL 14: 45-56). The publisher DOI page (10.1086/464037) is behind an automated-access block (not reachable by automated download). The article was obtained instead from the archive.org scan of IJAL 15(3), July 1949 (identifier sim_international-journal-of-american-linguistics_1949-07_15_3), where it occupies pp. 139-144 (PDF pages 1-6); the scanned text and PDF are saved in and logged in there.

readall_conflicts: The catalog (StressTyp2, 'StressTyp2') records Tewa as initial-stress (initial stress). The only listed work, Hoijer & Dozier 1949 (Santa Clara dialect), describes a four-tone system (high, middle, low, falling) and says explicitly that toned syllables bear 'about the same stress on each syllable', the only prosodic variation being pitch; the only reduced-stress syllables are toneless 'weak' syllables that are usually utterance-final. So the primary source and the catalog disagree on the type of prosodic system (tone plus non-culminative stress vs. fixed initial stress). The source is explicitly preliminary (one bilingual speaker, no phrasal-prosody data), and the basis of the StressTyp2 entry was not among the listed works, so the disagreement is recorded, not resolved.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and every supporting phrase in the record (pp. 75-77, p. 44) are verbatim on the page scan we hold of Speirs 1966; locator correct (printed p. 76 = p. 82). (2) Deciding source: a 1966 PhD dissertation that Glottolog types as the language's only grammar(-sketch) and that Sutton 2014 (held, opened now) calls the best published treatment of Tewa phonology; Sutton 2014:1028 independently states stem-initial lexical stress for Kiowa-Tanoan, confirming the root-initial reading behind our 'initial, dominant not strict' coding and the the primary-stress rule. No newer grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study of Tewa stress was found (Glottolog 45 refs; Crossref; Sutton's 2014 literature review says 21st-century academic work on Rio Grande Tewa is minimal and publication-restricted).

Tone, stress and intonation have not been sufficiently analyzed to be included in this text.
